title: Chapter 4 – Willow and Ink
html:
The problem with a miracle is that someone has to explain it.

Lin Jian spends the next twelve nights adding hundredths of a point to his dantian, one breath of the wheel at a time, and the days working out how a six-year-old boy with a five-element root can turn a bundle of willow bark into medicine without anyone asking how.

He settles on a book.

Notes on a Hundred Common Herbs is the most-thumbed volume in the family library: a thick, water-stained herbal written two centuries ago by a wandering doctor nobody remembers. On page forty-one, in a passage about white willow, the doctor complains that "the southern physicians have a method of purifying the bark by repeated washing and slow heat, which renders it a potent remedy for pain, but they guard it jealously and I could not learn it." That is all. One sentence. But it is a sentence anyone can find, and it gives a clever, stubborn child a reason to try.

So for eleven days he tries, where everyone can see him.

He borrows a clay pot from the kitchen. He strips bark from the white willows that grow along the stream at the foot of the hill, and Lin Yue, who is three now and follows him everywhere like a small determined shadow, helps him peel it, her tongue between her teeth. "For Father," she announces to anyone who asks, very seriously. "Brother is making medicine for Father."

The cooks laugh. Old Nan laughs. They let him use a corner of the kitchen hearth, and he boils bark in water, and strains it through cloth, and boils it again, and produces eleven days of brown, bitter, useless liquid that he solemnly pours out behind the woodpile each evening.

It is not wasted. Every failure is a brick in the wall of the story.

On the twelfth night, the panel finally shows what he needs.

```
Host Qi Reserve: 0.81
```

\ \ \*

He goes down to the kitchen before dawn, when the hearths are still banked and the cooks are still asleep, with a clean pot of water and the best of the bark Lin Yue helped him peel.

He has thought a great deal about how this will feel. He has fabricated things before, in his first life, ten thousand times, through the ARK-7's emitters and a wall of screens. He has never done it with his own body as the power source.

He lays his palms on either side of the pot, opens the blueprint, and confirms.

```
[Fabrication: Willow Bark Extract]
Inputs: confirmed
Required Qi: 0.80 / 0.81 available
Begin? Y
```

The cold in his dantian moves.

It does not drain away slowly, the way it leaves him when he scans. It pours, all at once, down his arms and out through his palms in a single smooth rush, and for one terrible heartbeat he understands how empty a person can be. The kitchen tilts.

Then a faint blue shimmer forms over the pot, the same blue he last saw in a sealed chamber in a world he will never see again. The bark in the water stirs. Its surface blurs. A fine white mist lifts out of it, thin as breath on a cold morning, and the water rises up into the mist to meet it, and for a moment the two of them hang above the pot together, turning slowly. Then they settle.

The light goes out.

In the bottom of the pot there is a teaspoon of fine white powder, damp at the edges. The bark lies beside it, pale and stringy and somehow emptied, as if it has been squeezed of everything it ever held.

```
[Fabrication Complete]
Product: Willow Bark Extract
Yield: 3.2 g
Purity: 97.4%
Fabrication Count: 1
```

Lin Jian sits down hard on the kitchen floor and puts his head between his knees until the world stops moving.

When it does, he gets up, takes the honey jar from the shelf, and rolls the powder with a little honey into nine pills the size of peas. He makes them small on purpose. His father is not a test subject, and the dose a body tolerates in this world may not be the dose it tolerated in his last one. One pill at night, he decides. Watch. Adjust.

He wraps them in a twist of clean paper and climbs back into bed before the cooks wake, and does not sleep.

\ \ \*

He gives his father the first pill that evening, at dinner, in front of everyone, because that is the only way.

"I made medicine," he says, and holds out the twist of paper.

The table goes quiet. Lin Feng snorts. Lin Hu says, "Is it made of mud?" and his mother cuffs him. Second Uncle smiles indulgently. Grandfather, at the head of the table, sets down his chopsticks and watches.

His father looks at the little brown pill in his son's palm, and at his son's face, and Lin Jian sees him decide. Not to believe that the pill will work. To believe that his son needs him to take it.

"Thank you, Jian," he says, and swallows it.

Nothing happens at dinner. Nothing happens during the evening, when Father goes to his desk as usual and Lin Jian lies awake listening for the scratch of the brush. It comes, and then it stops early, much earlier than usual. The lamp goes out.

His father sleeps until dawn. Then past dawn. Then until the middle of the morning, when Su Qinghe, alarmed, goes in to check on him and comes out again with an odd expression and says he is fine, he is only sleeping.

When Lin Wenyuan finally comes out into the courtyard, the sun is high. He stands at the top of the steps, blinking in the light like a man who has been underground for a long time. His left hand still trembles. The torn channels have not healed. Nothing in a willow tree could heal them. But the deep, grinding ache he has carried in his shoulder for ten years has dulled to something he can almost ignore, and for the first time in ten years he has slept through a night.

He finds his son by the woodpile, pretending to stack kindling.

He does not say anything. He crouches down, puts his arms around the boy, and holds him for a long time, while Lin Yue, who has followed Lin Jian to the woodpile as usual, pats her father's back with great seriousness and says, "See? I helped."

Over his father's shoulder, Lin Jian sees his grandfather watching from the veranda of the main hall, his pipe unlit in his hand. And at the kitchen door, his mother, with flour on her hands, watching too.

Neither of them says anything. Neither of them ever does.

\ \ \*

Second Uncle comes to see him three days later.

He finds Lin Jian in the library, reading the herbal, and sits down across from him with a pleasant sigh and a bag of candied plums.

"Your father tells me you've done something remarkable," he says. "Medicine from willow bark! The southern method. And you only six." He sets the plums down between them. "You know, Jian, the family shop in Willow Ford sells medicine as well as talismans. A good pain remedy would sell very well. The Zhao shop across the square has nothing like it. If you showed me how you did it, every step, I could have it made for the shop, and it would help the whole family."

His smile is warm. His Qi, to the edge of Lin Jian's growing sense of such things, is not. It is quick and hungry, like a fire looking for a draft.

"Every step?" Lin Jian asks.

"Every step."

"It's very boring," Lin Jian warns him.

"I don't mind boring."

So Lin Jian shows him. He shows him all eleven days: the bark, the pot, the boiling, the straining, the second boiling, the cloth, the slow heat over the banked coals. He shows him with great care and enthusiasm, and Second Uncle writes it all down in a small notebook with a silver pencil, and thanks him warmly, and gives him the plums.

Lin Jian watches him go.

Nine days later a hired man in the Willow Ford shop is still boiling bark, and the bark is still turning into bitter brown water. Second Uncle stops asking. At dinner, he remarks to no one in particular that Jian's medicine must have been a lucky accident: a good batch of bark, perhaps, or the right weather.

Lin Jian agrees that it must have been.

That evening, his grandfather calls him up onto the eastern wall.

The old man is sitting on the parapet with his pipe, looking out at the dark shape of the Beast Mountains, and for a while he says nothing at all. Lin Jian sits beside him and waits. He has learned that with his grandfather, waiting is a kind of conversation.

"Your Second Uncle asked you for your method," the old man says at last.

"Yes, Grandfather."

"And you showed him."

"I showed him everything I did in the kitchen."

His grandfather draws on the pipe. The coal glows and fades. "Everything you did in the kitchen," he repeats thoughtfully. He seems to turn the words over, the way he might turn over a stone to see what lives underneath. Then, to Lin Jian's surprise, he chuckles, low and dry.

"Good," he says. "That's good. In this family, little builder, we share everything." He taps the pipe out against the stone. "But nobody is obliged to share what happens in the dark before the cooks wake up."

Lin Jian goes very still.

His grandfather does not look at him. He stands, slowly, one hand on the parapet, and settles his robe. "If your Second Uncle asks you for anything else," he says, "you may show him whatever you like. And then you may come and tell me what he asked for." He pauses. "Only me."

He goes down the steps. Lin Jian stays on the wall a long time, watching the mountains, and wonders how much of what happens before the cooks wake up the old man has already seen.

He goes on making the pills every two weeks, at dawn, in the kitchen, when no one is awake but his mother, who has taken to rising early and sitting by the kitchen door with a cup of tea, looking at the courtyard and never once at the pot.

\ \ \*

The five-element root, for all its faults, buys him one thing he did not expect.

A child who may cultivate, however poorly, is entitled to lessons, and he has had his: the sensing breath and the first wheel, taught alone at dawn. What he has not had is the spell class. On the first morning of autumn, Uncle Mao decides he has waited long enough, sends Old Nan to fetch him from the library, and Lin Jian walks down into the courtyard and takes his place on the stones among the other children for the first time instead of above them on the roof.

Lin Hu sniggers. Lin Bo, who is thirteen now and at the third layer and has no reason to be kind to a six-year-old cousin, shifts over to make room for him and passes him half a rice cake without a word.

"Today," says Uncle Mao, "since the rest of you have forgotten everything I ever taught you, and since a certain young man has finished his breathing and may sit with us, we begin the spells again at the beginning." He holds up one hand, fingers spread. "A spell is a shape. Your Qi flows through your channels the way water flows through a field. A spell is a channel you dig on purpose, a path that turns that water into something else. Fire. A wall. A blade. The hand seals you learn are not magic words. They are the walls of the channel. Get them wrong, and the water spills out and does nothing."

Lin Jian sits very still, because this is the most important thing anyone in this world has said to him.

A spell is a circuit. Qi is the current. The channels are wires. The hand seals are switches, closing and opening paths in a precise order. A talisman is the same circuit drawn on paper in ink that can hold a charge, waiting for someone to close the last switch.

Every clan child in the Tianyuan Realm learns this at six. None of them, he suspects, has ever been taught to think of it as engineering.

"Every Lin child learns one art before any other," Uncle Mao goes on. "Not a fire. Not a sword. The Five-Element Ward Art. It closes small wounds. It costs very little. And it will save your life more often than any weapon, because a cut that closes is a cut that doesn't fester." He glances at Lin Jian. "It uses all five elements together. Most of you will manage the part that suits your root best, and the rest slowly. A five-element root can manage all of it, but not soon."

He shows them the seals. Five of them, one for each element, folded into one another in a sequence like the fingers of two hands lacing together. Then he takes a knife and draws it across the back of his own hand, not deeply, and makes the seals, and the cut closes before their eyes, leaving a thin pink line.

The children practice for the rest of the morning. Lin Bo, with his strong wood element, manages a faint green glow on his second try. Lin Hu, with fire and wood, manages a warmth that makes his cousin's scratched knuckle sting. Lin Shu, the quiet one, manages nothing at all, and bites his lip.

Lin Jian makes the seals once, slowly, and watches the Qi try to move.

It does exactly what it did on the first night: five threads trying to go through the circuit at once, grinding, scattering. Nothing happens. Lin Hu laughs.

He does it again. This time, as his fingers lace through the sequence, he does not let the elements in together. He feeds them one at a time, water through the water seal, wood through the wood, around the wheel, each element passing through its own gate in turn, the way they pass through his breathing.

It is like threading five needles in the dark. It takes everything he has.

On his knuckle, where he scraped it on the stones that morning, there is a faint flicker of light. Not green. Not blue. Something without a color, like heat shimmer over a summer road. The scrape closes.

When he looks up, Uncle Mao is watching him with no expression at all.

"Again," the old man says. "Tomorrow. And the day after. And every day after that."

Then he turns to Lin Shu and begins correcting his thumbs, and does not look at Lin Jian again for the rest of the lesson.

That night, Lin Jian sits in his room and looks at the panel's record of what happened.

```
[Host Spell Analysis: Five-Element Ward Art (Mortal Rank)]
Standard casting efficiency (host): 0%
Sequential casting efficiency (host): 22%
Note: Host's sequential method reduces interference. Efficiency will improve with practice and channel width.
```

Twenty-two percent. He is casting a healing spell built for five elements at once, one element at a time, through a root everyone says is too thin to cast it well.

He thinks about circuits for a long time.

\ \ \*

Autumn passes. He goes to lessons, and makes willow pills every two weeks, and breathes the wheel every night with his mother by the door.

He also starts spending his afternoons in Third Aunt's pill room, because no one else wants to.

It is a low, smoky room behind the kitchen with a single window, shelves of jars to the ceiling, and the bronze cauldron squatting over a bed of charcoal in the middle of the floor like a fat green toad. Third Aunt Wenqing works there alone most days, her sleeves tied back and her hair bound under a cloth, and for the first week she tolerates him the way she tolerates the kitchen cat.

"Grind that," she says, and points at a mortar full of dried ginseng root. "Finer. Finer than that. You want it like flour. If it's coarse it burns on the outside and stays raw in the middle, and then the whole batch is charcoal."

He grinds. He watches. On the eighth day she lets him feed the fire.

He learns the recipe without asking for it, which is how he learns everything: spirit ginseng, clear spring water, three grains of pine resin, a pinch of the gray moss that grows on the north side of the cliffs. He learns that the cauldron has to be warmed with Qi as well as charcoal, and that Third Aunt does it by laying her palms flat against the bronze and pushing her wood-element Qi into the metal until the green patina glows. He learns that she can hold that glow steady for the time it takes to recite the Breathing Method twice, and that the pills need three times that long.

"So you stop and start," he says.

"So I stop and start." She wipes her forehead with her wrist. "And every time I stop, the heat drops, and every time I start it jumps, and half of what's in there cooks and half of it burns. The Sect's alchemists have furnaces with formations that hold the heat even. Their Breath-Gathering Pills are sixty parts in a hundred good. Mine are thirty." She shrugs. "Ours are what we can afford, so ours are what we use."

He looks at the cauldron and thinks about temperature curves, and thermal mass, and the uneven, sputtering glow of a single tired woman's Qi holding a pot of herbs at heat for an hour.

That night he asks the panel the question he has been carrying around all week.

```
[Query: Breath-Gathering Pill (Level 1) — fabrication]
Recipe data: sufficient (observed)
Status: LOCKED
Requirement: Pill Synthesis (Interface Level 2)
```

Level two. Sixty-one points of Creation Energy away.

He lies awake for a while, doing arithmetic. Then he gets up and goes back to the wheel.

Third Aunt never asks why a six-year-old boy wants to spend his afternoons grinding roots in a smoky room. But on the last day of autumn she hands him a small cloth bag of the pills, eight of them, dark and bitter, and says gruffly, "A five-element root needs more help than most. Don't tell Lin Hu. He'll want some too."

He thanks her, and means it. Even at thirty parts in a hundred, it is more Qi than the wheel can pull out of the air in a week.

He learns the household's other arts by watching, the way he has always learned. The seals for the Fire Starter, which every servant in the house learns to activate even though not one of them can draw it. The quick twisting gesture the children use to make a whirlwind sweep the courtyard, which is not a spell for sweeping at all but a battle art called Cloudstep that knocks an enemy's feet out from under him, and which Uncle Mao makes them practice on leaves because, he says, a leaf forgives you and an enemy does not. The bronze arm-guards of Fourth Uncle's village guard, which he scans one afternoon when a farmer leaves his on a bench by the gate.

```
[Scan: Mantle Arm-Guard (Mortal Grade)]
Material: bronze, spirit copper inlay, blood-keyed activation glyph
Function: single-use barrier, renewable with ambient Qi over ~6 hours
Blueprint: Saved (partial)
Creation Energy +3 (39 / 100)
```

Spirit copper. A metal that carries Qi the way ordinary copper carries current. He files it away.

The farmer comes back for his arm-guard while Lin Jian is still sitting on the bench beside it, and Fourth Uncle comes with him, sweating from the drill, his practice sword over one shoulder.

"Don't play with those," Fourth Uncle says, not unkindly. He picks up the arm-guard and buckles it onto the farmer's forearm himself. "They bite."

"How does it work?" Lin Jian asks. "He doesn't cultivate."

Lin Wenshi looks at him with mild surprise, as if it has never occurred to him that anyone would ask. "Mortal grade," he says. "Made for men like Old Gou here. The refiner in Willow Ford puts the shape in it. All the wearer has to do is give it a drop of blood the first time, so it knows him, and a word when he needs it. Then the barrier draws on the Qi in the air for the rest." He slaps the farmer's shoulder. "Not much of a barrier. It'll turn an arrow or a wolf. It won't turn a cultivator's spell above the second layer." He nods at the farmer's sword, a plain straight blade with a thin line of copper set along the spine. "Same with the swords. They hold an edge of Qi if the man holding them has trained his body enough to feed them. Old Gou has been training for eight years. He can cut a post at a pace. On a good day."

"And a cultivator?"

"A cultivator of the fourth layer," Fourth Uncle says, "would kill Old Gou and me together before either of us got his sword up." He says it quite cheerfully. "That's why I keep thirty of them, little nephew. And why I keep them behind a wall." He ruffles Lin Jian's hair and goes back to the yard.

Old Gou, buckled up, grins down at the small boy on the bench with half his front teeth missing. "Your uncle's too modest," he says. "Last spring we killed a whole pack of wolves at the north fence without losing a man. Mortal grade or not." He taps the copper line on his sword. "Good enough for farmers."

Lin Jian watches him go, and thinks about thirty farmers with eight years of training and good enough weapons, and about what they would be with better ones.

On the night of the first snow, three months after his first lesson, the grain in his dantian swells, presses outward against something he cannot see, and breaks through it, quietly, like ice cracking on a pond.

```
[Host Status Update]
Qi Refining: Layer 2
Host Qi Reserve: 1.85
Channels opened: arms (4 / 4), chest (2 / 6)
Five-Gate Wheel efficiency: 21%
```

Lin Feng took two years to go from the first layer to the second. Lin Hu took nearly three.

His mother, by the door, opens her eyes. "Two?" she asks quietly.

He nods.

She is silent for a moment. "In the courtyard, you're still on the first layer," she says. "You'll stay on the first layer until summer. Understand?"

"Yes, Mother."

She looks at him for a long time in the gray snow-light from the window.

"The willow bark won't last forever," she says at last. "The trees along the stream are already half-stripped. And what you need, whatever it is you need," she says this very carefully, not looking at him, "it isn't growing on this hill." She stands. "When the snow melts, I'm taking you into the outer mountains. Past the terraces. It's time you learned what's out there."

"Grandfather won't allow it."

"Your grandfather," his mother says, "will allow it if I'm with you. I spent ten years in those mountains, Jian. I know what lives in them." She pauses in the doorway, a dark shape against the snow. "And I know what they take."

Then she is gone, and the door closes, and Lin Jian lies back in the dark with the cold Qi turning slowly in his belly and his panel glowing quietly behind his eyes.

```
Creation Energy: 39 / 100
Recommended: high-Qi organic material. Unscanned biomes available.
```

The mountains, then.
